Experimental evaluations on a self-collected multiuser CSI dataset show that CUTA-HAR consistently outperforms representative sequence modeling baselines under a leave-one-user-out evaluation protocol, achieving average test accuracy improvements of 2.0%–6.7%. Action-level analysis further shows that structured activities can be recognized reliably, while complex activities such as fall and pickup remain challenging due to larger cross-user motion variations. These results indicate the effectiveness of attention-guided temporal modeling for improving cross-user robustness in Wi-Fi CSI-based HAR.

title: Can Time-Series Foundation Models Enhance Wireless Sensing Data Analytics? An Empirical Study
venue: Communications in computer and information science

title: CausalFi: Causality-Based Cross-Domain Human Activity Recognition With Wi-Fi
abstract: WiFi-based human activity recognition (HAR) has demonstrated significant potential in diverse intelligent applications. However, sensitive to environmental factors, cross-domain WiFi channel state information (CSI) poses significant challenges in the generalization of HAR models across different environments. In this paper, the structural causal model (SCM) is introduced to model causal relationships among activities, latent variables, and CSI data, laying a solid foundation toward developing a domain-invariant model for WiFi-based HAR tasks. In this paper, we propose CausalFi, a novel framework that leverages causal inference to mitigate the confounding effects of latent variables, significantly improving generalization performance. Integrating novel feature selection and importance sampling algorithms as the condition and intervention operations, CausalFi can effectively identify the stable action-relevant features from WiFi CSI for activity recognition. Furthermore, a novel counterfactual style augmentation approach is proposed to increase the stylistic diversity of the training data, reducing the risk of biased data distributions even with limited training samples in source domains. We implement a prototype of CausalFi using commercial ASUS RT-AC86U WiFi devices and conduct extensive cross-domain experiments to validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. With an average recognition accuracy of 92.6%, CausalFi significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in complex cross-domain environments, confirming the practicality of our framework for real-world WiFi-based HAR applications. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Classroom-HAR: A Study on Generalization in Wi-Fi CSI Sensing Using Deep Learning
abstract: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using Wi-Fi Channel State Information (CSI) is a privacy-preserving alternative to camera-based systems. However, its deployment in complex, multipath-rich environments like classrooms remains challenging due to signal variability and a lack of robust generalization. In this work, we present a comprehensive study on the generalization capabilities of Deep Learning models for CSI-based sensing in educational settings. To lower the barrier to entry, we release a complete open-source platform, including low-cost ESP32 acquisition software, training scripts, and a novel dataset comprising 27 spatial-activity scenarios (9 discrete locations × 3 activity states) across 5 subjects. Rather than proposing a purely architectural advancement, our primary contribution is a rigorous investigation across three increasing levels of difficulty: (A) a randomized baseline sanity check, (B) strict temporal drift, and (C) leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-user validation. Our results demonstrate that while standard models achieve near-perfect accuracy under ideal conditions, they degrade significantly as temporal and biometric constraints tighten. Crucially, our results indicate that a hybrid architecture combining a 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with an Attention-enhanced Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM) achieves the highest overall accuracy. However, our investigation equally positions the standalone BiLSTM as a formidable, computationally simpler competitor, offering commendable resilience against the noise and domain shifts inherent in commercial IoT deployments.

title: Cross-Domain Continual Learning for Edge Intelligence in Wireless ISAC Networks
abstract: In wireless networks with integrated sensing and communications (ISAC), edge intelligence (EI) is expected to be developed at edge devices (ED) for sensing user activities based on channel state information (CSI). However, due to the CSI being highly specific to users’ characteristics, the CSI-activity relationship is notoriously domain dependent, essentially demanding EI to learn sufficient datasets from various domains in order to gain cross-domain sensing capability. This poses a crucial challenge owing to the EDs’ limited resources, for which storing datasets across all domains will be a significant burden. In this paper, we propose the EdgeCL framework, enabling the EI to continually learn-then-discard each incoming dataset, while remaining resilient to catastrophic forgetting. We design a transformer-based discriminator for handling sequences of noisy and nonequispaced CSI samples. Besides, we propose a distilled core-set based knowledge retention method with robustness-enhanced optimization to train the discriminator, preserving its performance for previous domains while preventing future forgetting. Experimental evaluations show that EdgeCL achieves 89% of performance compared to cumulative training while consuming only 3% of its memory, mitigating forgetting by 79%.

title: Cross-Domain Gesture Recognition Model for CSI: GestureNet-BiLSTM
venue: Lecture notes in networks and systems

title: Cross-Domain Heart Rate Estimation from Active mmWave to Passive Wi-Fi Radar
abstract: Noncontact vital sign monitoring has attracted considerable attention as a key enabling technology for a wide range of applications. In particular, millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar-based heart rate (HR) estimation has been actively investigated. However, such systems require dedicated transmitting hardware, which incurs additional cost and deployment overhead. In contrast, passive Wi-Fi radar (PWR) exploits existing Wi-Fi access points (APs) as opportunistic illuminators, thereby enabling low-cost noncontact monitoring without requiring an additional transmitter. Nevertheless, prior PWR-based monitoring studies have primarily focused on human activity recognition and respiration rate estimation, while studies on HR estimation remain scarce. This research gap has also resulted in a lack of publicly available PWR datasets suitable for training HR estimation models. Motivated by these observations, we propose a PWR-based HR estimation model for resting adults, together with a training strategy that effectively transfers knowledge from publicly available mmWave radar datasets. First, we introduce a radar domain generalization transform (RDGT), which converts mmWave radar data into a PWR-like domain by accounting for the physical differences between the two sensing modalities. Second, we develop an HR estimation model that reduces the residual domain gap between the RDGT-transformed data and real PWR measurements. Experimental results on real PWR measurements show that the proposed method outperforms PWR-based respiration monitoring methods, signal processing-based HR estimation methods, and deep learning-based methods incorporating domain generalization.

title: Cross-Domain Multi-Person Human Activity Recognition via Near-Field Wi-Fi Sensing
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Wi-Fi-based human activity recognition (HAR) provides substantial convenience and has emerged as a thriving research field, yet the coarse spatial resolution inherent to Wi-Fi significantly hinders its ability to distinguish multiple subjects. By exploiting the near-field domination effect, establishing a dedicated sensing link for each subject through their personal Wi-Fi device offers a promising solution for multi-person HAR under native traffic. However, due to the subject-specific characteristics and irregular patterns of near-field signals, HAR neural network models require fine-tuning (FT) for cross-domain adaptation, which becomes particularly challenging with certain categories unavailable. In this paper, we propose WiAnchor, a novel training framework for efficient cross-domain adaptation in the presence of incomplete activity categories. This framework processes Wi-Fi signals embedded with irregular time information in three steps: during pre-training, we enlarge inter-class feature margins to enhance the separability of activities; in the FT stage, we innovate an anchor matching mechanism for cross-domain adaptation, filtering subject-specific interference informed by incomplete activity categories, rather than attempting to extract complete features from them; finally, the recognition of input samples is further improved based on their feature-level similarity with anchors. We construct a comprehensive dataset to thoroughly evaluate WiAnchor, achieving over 90% cross-domain accuracy with absent activity categories under multi-person scenarios.

title: Cross-Modal WiFi Sensing for Robot Activity Recognition
venue: 2026 9th International Conference on Intelligent Robotics and Control Engineering (IRCE)
abstract: Cross-modal technology leverages Channel State Information (CSI) to capture subtle environmental changes, offering a non-intrusive, low-cost, and illumination-independent paradigm for robotic perception. This paper systematically reviews the research progress at the intersection of WiFi sensing and robotics, with a focus on the key challenges in this field: traditional vision- and LiDAR-based solutions suffer from privacy risks, line-of-sight constraints, and high deployment costs, while WiFi signals, despite their unique advantages, are limited by signal instability, data annotation difficulties, and insufficient cross-scenario generalization. To address these issues, we propose a cross-modal robotic perception framework that integrates WiFi CSI, video, and audio, and design a Bidirectional Vision Transformer-Concatenated (BiVTC) model optimized for robot activity recognition. Experimental validation on the public RoboFiSense dataset [9] demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves 98.7% accuracy on an eight-class robot activity recognition task, significantly outperforming traditional machine learning methods. This paper further discusses the application prospects of cross-modal WiFi sensing in scenarios such as robotic SLAM, human-robot collaboration safety monitoring, and multi-robot systems, and identifies future research opportunities in cross-device collaborative sensing and integrated sensing and communication.

title: Cross-domain generalization in non-stationary data-based Human Activity Recognition
Cross-domain neural alignment (CDNA): A deep supervised domain adaptation in human activity recognition using device-free sensing
abstract: Wi-Fi sensor networks have grown rapidly due to their scalability and high data throughput, finding applications in tasks like tracking human motion in laboratory settings. These systems detect motion by analyzing fluctuations in radio signals caused by target movements, which generate identifiable activity patterns. However, their performance is influenced by factors such as environmental changes, unseen target subjects, multi-target tracking, data configurations, and the nature of target activities. These challenges lead to domain shifts between the training and testing phases, a common issue in real-world scenarios known as the domain-shifting problem in transfer learning. We propose a supervised domain alignment technique to address domain shifts in Wi-Fi sensor Channel State Information (CSI) datasets using minimal labeled target data. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art adversarial models trained on similar data, achieving superior cross-domain prediction accuracy. Evaluations on two public CSI datasets show consistent improvements, with an average Micro-F1 score of 90% for cross-user tasks and 67% for cross-user and cross-environment tasks using only 70 labeled target samples. This approach demonstrates its effectiveness in enhancing prediction accuracy under challenging domain shift scenarios.

title: CrossAR: Cross-Modal Contrastive Learning for WiFi-Vision Human Activity Recognition
abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) is a foundational technique that supports applications ranging from healthcare to smart homes. For nonintrusive and device-free HAR, human features can be extracted from WiFi channel state information (CSI) without cameras or on-body sensors. However, CSI data with fine-grained labels are scarce due to the need for laborious human annotations, hindering the generalization of WiFi-based HAR. Consequently, most HAR models rely on the supervision of coarse labels (e.g., “walking”, “running”), limiting the utility of WiFi-based HAR, which requires detailed knowledge to distinguish activities with subtle discrepancies. In this article, we propose CrossAR, a WiFi-Vision HAR approach based on self-supervised contrastive learning to fully exploit unlabeled data without human annotations. To tackle the coarse labels, CrossAR pioneers the contrast between unlabeled CSI and auxiliary labels from pretrained vision models as cross-modal supervision. Given the structure differences between CSI and auxiliary labels, we further devise a dual-stream dilated multilayer perceptron (D2MLP) and establish D2MLP-Nets as the backbone of CrossAR. Experimentally, we deploy off-the-shelf WiFi devices to construct a multiuser dataset for evaluation. On this new dataset and two public datasets, CrossAR outperforms state-of-the-art methods and achieves over 96.78% accuracy.

title: D-Sense: Expanding Gesture Recognition via Wi-Fi
abstract: Ubiquitous Wi-Fi signals capture rich spatiotemporal features of human gestures. Existing approaches to cross-domain gesture recognition typically either suppress domain-specific information, such as user identity, orientation, and location, or attempt to extract domain-invariant gesture features. However, these strategies often compromise task-level generalization capability and computational efficiency. To address this limitation, we propose D-Sense, a multi-task sensing system built on Channel State Information (CSI). First, leveraging the geometric properties of Doppler frequency, we establish a sensing area model. Based on this model, we introduce a physically interpretable multi-task cross-domain feature termed the Absolute Distance Profile (ADP). Similar to Doppler Frequency Shift (DFS), ADP captures gesture dynamics while simultaneously decoupling and preserving domain-related attributes. To jointly optimize multiple tasks, a lightweight Deep Neural Network (DNN) is adopted, and a Dynamic Weighting Mechanism (DWM) is incorporated to balance inter-task interactions during training. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that D-Sense achieves joint recognition accuracies of 97.38% for gesture recognition, 94.87% for user identification, 93.46% for orientation recognition, and 85.22% for localization. In cross-location settings, average gesture and user recognition accuracies range from 84.83% to 88.83% and 76.33% to 86.33%, respectively, while in cross-orientation settings, the corresponding accuracies range from 61.50% to 85.17% and 68.67% to 80.67%, indicating robust generalization across varying spatial configurations.

title: DACNet: A Robust Framework for Cross-Domain Wi-Fi Based Human Activity Recognition
DATTA: Domain-Adversarial Test-Time Adaptation for Cross-Domain WiFi-Based Human Activity Recognition
venue: IEEE Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision
abstract: WiFi-based human activity recognition (HAR) faces significant challenges in cross-domain generalization due to dynamic environmental variations, device heterogeneity, and subtle changes in human behavior. In this paper, we introduce DATTA – Domain-Adversarial Test-Time Adaptation – a novel framework that combines domain-adversarial training (DAT) with test-time adaptation (TTA) and a random weight-resetting mechanism. Unlike previous approaches that apply these techniques in isolation, DATTA is specifically tailored for WiFi-based HAR: it leverages DAT to learn robust, domain-invariant features while TTA continuously refines the model on streaming data. To mitigate catastrophic forgetting during adaptation, we incorporate a weight-resetting mechanism, ensuring sustained performance over prolonged domain shifts. Our extensive experiments on the Widar3.0-G6D dataset demonstrate that DATTA not only outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to 8.1% in F1-Score but also achieves real-time inference with a lightweight architecture, making it a compelling solution for practical WiFi sensing applications. The PyTorch implementation of DATTA is publicly available at: https://github.com/StrohmayerJ/DATTA.

title: DUAL-Net: Joint Domain-Invariant and User-Adaptive Feature Learning for Gesture Recognition
abstract: Human activity recognition has become an important component of human-computer interaction and ubiquitous computing. Among various sensing technologies, WiFi-based gesture recognition has attracted increasing attention due to its contactless nature and robustness to visual occlusion. However, environmental variations and user-specific differences often lead to significant performance degradation, particularly in cross-user scenarios. Existing methods primarily focus on learning domain-invariant representations, which may overlook user-specific characteristics that are essential for accurate recognition. To address this issue, we propose the Domain-invariant and User-Adaptive Learning Network (DUAL-Net), a dual-branch framework that jointly models domain-invariant and user-adaptive representations. Specifically, DUAL-Net incorporates a contrastive fusion learning (CFL) module with modality-specific encoders to learn complementary representations from WiFi and vision modalities. Furthermore, a spatial matrix difference (SMD)-guided cross-modal generation (CMG) module is introduced to generate user-adaptive WiFi features by incorporating structural priors derived from skeletal representations. To improve deployment efficiency, DUAL-Net adopts a two-stage learning framework, where adaptation is conducted offline to reduce online computational overhead. Experiments on the MM-Fi dataset and a self-collected dataset show that DUAL-Net achieves superior cross-user recognition performance compared with existing single-modality and multimodal methods. In addition, SMD-guided conditioning improves recognition accuracy by up to 8.79% over diffusion generation without structural guidance.

title: Deep Learning-Enhanced Human Sensing with Channel State Information: A Survey
abstract: With the growing advancement of wireless communication technologies, WiFi-based human sensing has gained increasing attention as a non-intrusive and device-free solution. Among the available signal types, Channel State Information (CSI) offers fine-grained temporal, frequency, and spatial insights into multipath propagation, making it a crucial data source for human-centric sensing. Recently, the integration of deep learning has significantly improved the robustness and automation of feature extraction from CSI in complex environments. This paper provides a comprehensive review of deep learning-enhanced human sensing based on CSI. We first outline mainstream CSI acquisition tools and their hardware specifications, then provide a detailed discussion of preprocessing methods such as denoising, time–frequency transformation, data segmentation, and augmentation. Subsequently, we categorize deep learning approaches according to sensing tasks—namely detection, localization, and recognition—and highlight representative models across application scenarios. Finally, we examine key challenges including domain generalization, multi-user interference, and limited data availability, and we propose future research directions involving lightweight model deployment, multimodal data fusion, and semantic-level sensing.

title: Deep Sequential Modeling of WiFi Channel State Information for Human Activity Recognition
abstract: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) enables device-free indoor sensing without cameras or wearables. We compare four deep sequential models on this task-a vanilla Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), and a hybrid that feeds a 1D Residual Network (ResNet1D) front-end into stacked GRU layers. Two public datasets are used: a single-subject set with 69,000 samples covering seven activities across three rooms, and a multi-subject set with 3,000 samples from thirty subjects performing five activities. To support reproducibility, the preprocessing pipeline, input dimensions, and hyperparameters are reported in full, and each model is trained over five random seeds with mean and standard deviation reported. An ablation isolates the contribution of the convolutional front-end, the residual connections, and the recurrent stack. The hybrid GRU+ResNet1D reaches 99.68 ± 0.05% on the single-subject set and 92.62 ± 0.41% on the multi-subject set under subject-dependent evaluation, exceeding the GRU baseline by 4.64% on the harder set. We discuss the hardware requirements for CSI extraction, the challenge of separating motion from environmental drift, and the privacy properties that make the approach an enabler-rather than a substitute-for identity-aware security systems.

title: Descriptor: The WiFi-Based Human Activity Recognition Under Everyday Life Changes Dataset (WiFi-Wild)
abstract: WiFi-based human activity recognition (HAR) provides a non-invasive alternative to camera- and wearable-based sensing, but model performance often degrades under environmental and subject-specific variations. This work introduces the WiFi-Wild dataset, a publicly available collection of WiFi channel state information (CSI) signals designed to capture everyday life changes such as furniture rearrangement, transmitter/receiver placement, device interference, and subject diversity. The WiFi-Wild dataset was collected in a residential environment using ESP32 devices, with a single participant performing a range of daily activities under multiple spatial and environmental scenarios, and additional participant appearances were included to evaluate subject variability. To demonstrate dataset utility, a hybrid deep learning model combining a convolutional neural network (CNN) with an attention-based bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) network was trained for activity classification and evaluated across different configurations. Results show that environmental and subject-related variations substantially affect model performance, with furniture rearrangements and TX/RX repositioning reducing F1-scores by up to 21%, and signal interference or clothing changes causing decreases of 7%–12%. The WiFi-Wild dataset enables systematic, reproducible evaluation of WiFi-based HAR models under realistic conditions and supports the development of more robust systems. IEEE SOCIETY/COUNCIL Signal Processing Society (SPS) DATA TYPE/LOCATION Time-series; Ireland DATA DOI/PID 10.5281/zenodo.18431784

title: Descriptor: WiFi-Granular Activities in Kitchen Dataset (Wi-GRAK)
abstract: This article introduces a comprehensive, multimodal dataset designed for advancing device-free human activity recognition in kitchen environments. The dataset concurrently captures both WiFi channel state information (CSI) and received signal strength indicator (RSSI) data, enabling analysis at varying levels of detail. It encompasses nine distinct single-person activities, systematically categorized into three fine-grained (e.g., precise utensil movements), three mid-grained (e.g., combining ingredients), and three coarse-grained (e.g., meal preparation) actions. To ensure robustness and diversity, data was collected from three different users, across three separate environmental settings, utilizing a pair of ESP32 microcontrollers as transmitter and receiver. Each unique activity scenario was repeated over 10 trials, resulting in a total of 1620 structured data entries. This dataset serves as a valuable benchmark for developing and evaluating machine learning models, particularly in exploring the comparative advantages of using CSI and RSSI for granular activity classification in real-world settings. IEEE SOCIETY/COUNCIL Instrumentation and Measurement DATA TYPE/LOCATION 2.4 GHz WiFi Packets; Personal Home, Thunder Bay, Canada DATA DOI/PID 10.21227/8ps2-vz31

title: DisCo: Disentangled Representation Learning for Edge-Terminal Collaborative WiFi Sensing
abstract: WiFi sensing is attractive for human activity recognition, behavior monitoring, and intelligent IoT due to its contact free, low-cost, and ease of deployment. However, WiFi sensing systems often suffer from limited cross-domain generalization, a tight cost-latency trade-off on resource-constrained terminals, and unreliable on-device inference in dynamic environments. We propose DisCo, an edge-terminal collaborative WiFi sensing framework that jointly targets cross-domain robustness, reliable inference, and efficient deployment. DisCo enhances generalization through disentangled representation learning and style augmentation. To support efficient deployment, DisCo uses deployment-oriented distillation for lightweight terminal inference and embedding-level edge refinement. During inference, it triggers collaboration based on prediction reliability and uploads compact embeddings only when terminal predictions are unreliable, thereby reducing uplink overhead and end-to-end latency while maintaining accuracy. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that DisCo achieves competitive performance in accuracy, cross-domain generalization, robustness to dynamic disturbances, and system efficiency, while achieving reliable collaborative inference with a low upload ratio.

title: DoRF++: Spherical Representation Learning over Doppler Radiance Fields for Robust Wi-Fi Sensing
abstract: Motivated by the IEEE 802.11bf effort to standardize advanced WLAN sensing, interest in Wi-Fi Channel State Information (CSI) for passive, device-free, and privacy-preserving activity and gesture recognition has grown rapidly. Recent studies have shown that Doppler velocity projections extracted from CSI, which directly reflect human-motion velocity, enable more robust human activity recognition (HAR) and stronger generalization across users and unseen conditions. Nevertheless, reliable generalization under real-world variability remains a major challenge that hinders the adoption of Wi-Fi sensing. To address this challenge, we build on Doppler Radiance Fields (DoRF), adapting the concept of neural radiance fields (NeRF) from computer vision to Wi-Fi sensing. DoRF treats the extracted Doppler velocity projections as sparse virtual-camera views of human motion. From these views it recovers a regularized latent 3-D motion descriptor whose projections along learned effective Doppler directions explain the CSI observations. The recovered motion is then re-projected onto an equiangular grid of directions on the unit sphere, yielding a spherical representation of the underlying activity. Because DoRF produces a signal defined on the sphere, this paper introduces DoRF++, a spherical representation-learning model that applies quadrature-aware spherical Transformers directly to the spherical field for activity classification. Experiments on our collected hand-gesture dataset show that DoRF++ noticeably outperforms state-of-the-art Wi-Fi-based HAR methods in cross-user generalization accuracy, especially for difficult gestures when only a single multi-antenna receiver access point (AP) is available.

title: Dual-Axis Transformer-GNN Framework for Touchless Finger Location Sensing by Using Wi-Fi Channel State Information
abstract: Camera, lidar, and wearable-based gesture recognition technologies face practical limitations such as lighting sensitivity, occlusion, hardware cost, and user inconvenience. Wi-Fi channel state information (CSI) can be used as a contactless alternative to capture subtle signal variations caused by human motion. However, existing CSI-based methods are highly sensitive to domain shifts and often suffer notable performance degradation when applied to environments different from the training conditions. To address this issue, we propose a domain-robust touchless finger location sensing framework that operates reliably even in a single-link environment composed of commercial Wi-Fi devices. The proposed system applies preprocessing procedures to reduce noise and variability introduced by environmental factors and introduces a multi-domain segment combination strategy to increase the domain diversity during training. In addition, the dual-axis transformer learns temporal and spatial features independently, and the GNN-based integration module incorporates relationships among segments originating from different domains to produce more generalized representations. The proposed model is evaluated using CSI data collected from various users and days; experimental results show that the proposed method achieves an in-domain accuracy of 99.31% and outperforms the best baseline by approximately 4% and 3% in cross-user and cross-day evaluation settings, respectively, even in a single-link setting. Our work demonstrates a viable path for robust, calibration-free finger-level interaction using ubiquitous single-link Wi-Fi in real-world and constrained environments, providing a foundation for more reliable contactless interaction systems.

title: ESP32 WiFi-Sensing to Enable Few-Shot Human Activity Recognition in Building Automation
abstract: Non-invasive Wi-Fi sensing using Channel State Information (CSI) provides an anonymous and device-free approach to Human Activity Recognition (HAR), enabling a range of building automation services, such as Ambient Intelligence-Assisted Living, visual comfort through adaptive lighting, and energy-efficient HVAC control. However, deploying these systems across different environments within the same building remains challenging, as traditional machine learning models require complete retraining when applied to new environments or when furniture layouts are modified. To overcome this cross-domain limitation, we propose a CNN-based prototypical few-shot transfer learning approach that leverages the nonlinear features learned in a source environment and adapts only the linear output (fully connected) layer to previously unseen target environments using a small amount of target-domain data (few-shot learning). A low-cost sensor network consisting of six single-antenna ESP32 modules communicating via the ESP-NOW protocol was implemented in two adjacent rooms at LARA/UnB, featuring substantially different furniture layouts. The proposed system achieved a target-domain transfer accuracy of 73.48%, demonstrating that low-costWi-Fi sensing combined with few-shot transfer learning provides a practical, privacy-preserving solution for intelligent building automation.

title: EchoCSI: A Systematic Cross-Environment Benchmark and a Frozen-Prior Vector-Quantized Recipe for WiFi CSI-to-Image Generation
abstract: WiFi Channel State Information (CSI)-based human image generation offers privacy-preserving sensing, but existing methods trained in one physical environment degrade sharply in unseen rooms. We attribute this to multipath propagation: static, environment-dependent reflections and dynamic, person-dependent reflections are entangled in conventional CSI encoders. We propose EchoCSI (Echo-Informed Domain-Generalizable WiFi Imaging), which combines 1) an encoder that couples time-domain CSI with Channel Impulse Response (CIR) features through cross-attention conditioning, 2) vector-quantization (VQ) with domain-adversarial and orthogonality losses that build a discrete, domain-invariant representation, and 3) a two-variant design—EchoCSI-Q (Quality) and EchoCSI-H (Hybrid), both keeping the Stable Diffusion VAE decoder frozen—that offers a light design point and a stronger default. We also formalize a Leave-One-Environment-Out (LOEO) protocol on MM-Fi and report multi-seed results with a clean, all-fold factorial ablation. We are explicit about scope: our evidence is confined to MM-Fi’s four indoor environments, which share a single laboratory floorplan with different furniture configurations, so the cross-environment claims here concern furniture-/layout-level shift within one building rather than generalization across arbitrary unseen buildings. With 12 runs per model (3 seeds  $\times 4$  folds), EchoCSI-H attains the best Target SSIM (0.241, vs. LatentCSI 0.209), the best DG Gap (11.3%,  $\sim 2.4\times $  lower than LatentCSI’s 27.5% and  $\sim 3.3\times $  lower than Wi2Vi’s 37.0%), and the best Target FID (11.4), improving all three axes simultaneously. A full-corpus re-evaluation on all 40 subjects and 27 actions of MM-Fi (60 additional runs) confirms the advantage at scale: EchoCSI-H’s Target SSIM rises to 0.257, exceeding every baseline ( $p\lt 0.001$ , paired, Bonferroni-corrected). A cross-dataset leave-one-room-out evaluation on WiMANS—a second paired CSI–RGB corpus with different rooms and different WiFi hardware, connected through a fixed training-free input adapter—reproduces the ranking: EchoCSI-H again attains the best Target SSIM and FID. Our factorial ablation yields a decomposition we report honestly, including where it corrected our own earlier assumptions: spatial VQ discretization drives the low DG Gap, the frozen SD image prior—not decoder fine-tuning, which we find hurts target-environment quality—provides absolute quality, and the CIR branch and the domain-adversarial/orthogonality losses have only second-order effects on this benchmark. EchoCSI-Q, a lighter frozen-decoder variant, reaches Target SSIM 0.201 and Target FID 13.4 and matches the learned-decoder baselines on absolute quality.

title: Evidential Deep Learning for Open-Set Wi-Fi-Based Human Activity Recognition With Semi-Supervised Domain Adaptation
abstract: Most existing research on wireless human activity recognition (WHAR) algorithms operates under a closed-set assumption. This limits their applicability in real-world scenarios where the presence of unseen or unknown activities is inevitable. To address this limitation, distance-based and prototype-based approaches have been proposed to detect the unknown activity classes. However, these approaches assume that all known activity classes remain in-distribution across domains, which is not the case in WHAR. This paper introduces an open-set Wi-Fi-based HAR framework, Wi-EDL, based on evidential deep learning (EDL). The framework quantifies categorical evidence to accurately discriminate between known and unknown channel state information patterns. Instead of just predicting probabilities, Wi-EDL learns to predict evidence for each activity class. A novel adversarial learning approach is applied between the feature extractor and domain classifier to enhance generalization performance in both closed-set and open-set recognition tasks. Furthermore, a semi-supervised domain adaptation technique (SSDA) adapts the model trained on source domains to target domains. This enhances cross-domain robustness and reduces overconfidence in false predictions. To eliminate the need for manual threshold adjustment and enable accurate rejection of unknown activities in each target domain, an adaptive threshold determination mechanism (ATDM) is proposed to dynamically establish class-specific thresholds. Experimental results demonstrate that Wi-EDL exhibits superior performance in both closed-set (approximately 98.43%) and open-set scenarios across six target domains, with average AURC of 0.0749 and AUROC of 0.8376. Compared with three state-of-the-art methods, Wi-EDL achieves the highest AURC reductions of 0.5862, 0.3740, and 0.3104, respectively, in target domains.

title: Federated Few-Shot Prototypical Learning for Personalized WiFi-Based Human Activity Recognition
abstract: Wi-Fi channel state information (CSI) has emerged as a promising alternative to wearable sensors for passive human activity recognition (HAR). However, its sensitivity to environmental layouts and device heterogeneity leads to highly non-IID data across users. Also, combined with the limited number of labeled CSI samples available on each device, existing federated learning (FL) approaches often suffer from representation drift and poor convergence. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a federated few-shot learning framework that incorporates prototypical learning to promote consistent and discriminative CSI embeddings across clients. Each client extracts magnitude–phase statistical features, conducts episodicN-wayK-shot training, and updates its local encoder using a prototypical loss. Unlike FedAvg, the server employs an Adam-based aggregation strategy that integrates prototype-induced parameter updates, providing more stable global alignment under heterogeneous data distributions. Experiments on a multi-configuration CSI dataset demonstrate that the proposed federated prototypical learning method significantly improves recognition accuracy, training stability, and cross-environment generalization compared with state-of-the-art FL baselines. These results highlight the potential of few-shot prototypical learning as a scalable and robust solution for CSI-based human activity recognition.

title: Gesture Recognition Using WiFi Channel State Information: Challenges and Insights
InSSeqTra: Inter Data Selective Sequential Transfer Learning for Domain Adaptation in CSI-Based HAR
Input-Modality-Oriented Human Activity Recognition: A Systematic Review of Sensing Technologies, Learning Architectures, and Deployment Challenges
Internal Response-Guided Test-Time Adaptation for Cross-Location CSI-Based Human Activity Recognition
venue: International Conference on Communication, Remote Sensing and Information Technology (CRSIT)
abstract: WiFi Channel State Information (CSI)-based human activity recognition has attracted increasing attention due to its non-contact, privacy-preserving, and low-cost sensing capability. However, CSI-based models often suffer from performance degradation when deployed at unseen test locations, because indoor layout changes, multipath propagation, and position offsets may cause distribution shifts between training and testing data. To address this problem, this paper proposes an internal response-guided test-time adaptation framework for cross-location CSI-based human activity recognition. The proposed method focuses on the deployment stage and exploits prediction distributions, temporal attention responses, and dynamic gating outputs generated during inference. These internal responses are used to select reliable target-domain samples and guide lightweight online adaptation without requiring target-domain labels. Prediction consistency and temporal attention consistency are further introduced to improve adaptation stability, while only a small subset of parameters is updated to reduce the risk of model drift. Experiments on the Widar3.0 cross-location setting show that the proposed method improves the average recognition accuracy from 91.87% to 93.23%. The results indicate that model internal responses can provide effective adaptation cues for robust cross-location CSI sensing.

title: Learning Motion-Induced Channel Dynamics with Multiresolution Multiplex Graphs for Wi-Fi CSI-Based Human Activity Sensing
abstract: Wi-Fi channel state information (CSI) supports human activity recognition from motion-induced changes in indoor propagation, yet device, environment, and user changes perturb both channel responses and subcarrier relations. We present a model that aligns valid subcarriers across inputs and combines CSI response features with a multiresolution graph. Temporal decomposition produces residual components at multiple resolutions and a smooth component. The graph propagates information along positive and negative relations between subcarriers within each resolution and uses signal energy to guide propagation across resolutions. A gate incorporates the graph representation into the response classifier. A controlled multipath study further tests the physical interpretation of signed amplitude correlations. Experiments on CSI-Bench yield weighted-F1 scores of 95.96%, 50.16%, 44.08%, and 52.19% on the four protocols, with a cross-domain mean of 48.81%, exceeding the strongest of ten locally reevaluated baselines by 4.84 points.

title: Leveraging Graph Attention Embedding and Mutual Prompting for CSI Drift Suppression Localization
abstract: This work addresses the challenges of feature redundancy, fingerprint drift, and insufficient matching robustness in Channel State Information (CSI)-based fingerprint matching and indoor positioning. To address these issues, we propose a feature optimization and matching algorithm based on a graph attention mechanism. Firstly, a Graph Attention Network (GAT)–Variational Graph Auto-Encoder (VGAE) graph embedding model is developed to adaptively allocate node weights, enhancing feature discriminability and generalizability. Secondly, the domain-agnostic mutual prompting (DAMP) strategy is introduced to achieve robust cross-domain distribution matching through bidirectional mutual feature alignment, effectively suppressing CSI drift. Finally, the FM index-based alignment algorithm (FMAlign), inspired by biological sequences, is employed for fast anchor segment matching of embedded fingerprints, thereby improving the accuracy and robustness of the localization process. Experimental results show a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 1.95 m and an average positioning error of 0.57 m. The method demonstrates high efficiency and stability in feature optimization, drift suppression, and sequence matching, providing a reliable solution for high-precision indoor positioning.

title: Low-latency domain-adaptive human activity recognition using Wi-Fi: A Doppler-guided raw CSI contrastive learning approach
abstract: Existing Wi-Fi networks are being transformed into intelligent sensing platforms, which enable device-free, passive, and privacy-preserving wireless human activity recognition (WHAR). Despite this potential, real-world deployments of Wi-Fi-based HAR systems are still hindered by two primary challenges: environment-induced domain shifts and high post-window processing latency. These factors increase prediction errors in previously unseen environments and also introduce significant delays in post-incident detection. To address these issues, this work proposes a framework that integrates supervised contrastive learning (SCL), knowledge distillation (KD), and domain adaptation (DA). Specifically, Doppler traces derived from channel state information (CSI) are combined with raw CSI to create contrastive pairs, enabling the CSI encoder to fuse activity-discriminative information into its representations. Following the SCL module, a KD module is developed to transfer both intra-class and inter-class relational structures from the Doppler-trace-based teacher model to the raw CSI-based student model, and DA then adapts the CSI-based model to target domains. During inference, the framework operates directly on the CSI amplitude and phase, eliminating the need for computationally expensive preprocessing. Experimental results show that the proposed framework reduces the post-window processing latency from 8.60 s to 0.14 s by eliminating Doppler-trace computation. Under this low-latency setting, the proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, achieving average accuracies of 86.80% and 97.21% with only 1% and 5% labeled target-domain data for DA. By achieving real-time inference, the proposed framework paves the way for practical deployments of WHAR in time-critical applications, such as healthcare monitoring, smart homes, and real-time human-machine interaction.

title: MORIC: CSI Delay-Doppler Decomposition for Robust Wi-Fi-based Human Activity Recognition
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: The newly established IEEE 802.11bf Task Group aims to amend the WLAN standard to support advanced sensing applications such as human activity recognition (HAR). Although studies have demonstrated the potential of sub-7 GHz Wi-Fi Channel State Information (CSI) for HAR, existing methods often degrade substantially under realistic variations across users, environments, and sensing configurations. This work addresses the poor generalization of Wi-Fi-based HAR by extracting motion-centered representations that reduce dependence on static, environment-specific, and non-activity-related CSI magnitude and phase patterns. CSI signals are transformed into the delay-profile space and decomposed into multiple Doppler velocity projections, which are modeled as observations of a moving point's velocity from different unknown directions, analogous to virtual cameras observing the same motion with varying degrees of clarity. This yields a richer activity representation than either a single aggregated Doppler estimate or the spurious, environment-dependent CSI patterns used in prior works. Since these projections are unordered and may recur due to random multipath propagation, we introduce MORIC, a novel order- and repetition-invariant time-series classification model for robust Wi-Fi-based HAR. Experimental results on the collected dataset show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in cross-user hand motion recognition, especially for challenging gestures. Incorporating only a few calibration samples further improves accuracy, demonstrating MORIC's adaptability and highlighting the potential of the proposed methodology for practical Wi-Fi sensing in real-world scenarios.

title: MS-MBSP: Multi-Scale Multi-Band Spectral Pooling for Device-Free Wi-Fi CSI Respiratory State Classification
abstract: Wi-Fi Channel State Information (CSI) is a contactless sensing modality that captures respiratory chest motion through subcarrier-wise amplitude variation. This paper presents MS-MBSP (Multi-Scale Multi-Band Spectral Pooling), a CNN-BiLSTM-based configuration for device-free five-class respiratory state classification, including NORMAL, SLOW, FAST, HOLD, and COUGH. MS-MBSP introduces two structural components: multi-band spectral pooling that separates respiratory and cough-related frequency regions, and a dual-scale branch that processes time-aligned 5 s and 10 s windows. An auxiliary respiratory-rate regression head based on PSD-peak pseudo-labels is additionally used as a mild training-time regularizer; removing it changes the 90-fold mean Macro F1 by only  $\Delta =+0.006$  (paired Wilcoxon  $p=0.333$ ), so it is not a performance-driving component. The method is evaluated on a 10-subject Wi-Fi CSI dataset using a subject-disjoint validation rotation protocol, where the training, validation, and test subjects are mutually separated across 90 folds. Under identical training settings, we compare MS-MBSP with three time-series baselines and four spectral-pooling variants, including spec, spec_large, multi_band_5s, and multi_band_10s. MS-MBSP achieves a 90-fold mean Macro F1 of 0.7612 and an accuracy of 0.8129. The parameter-controlled spec_large variant shows little improvement over spec, indicating that the gain mainly comes from the proposed structural design rather than parameter count. Per-class and confusion-matrix analyses show that the multi-band and multi-scale components improve COUGH and SLOW classification while residual errors remain mainly between NORMAL, SLOW, and HOLD. Classical spectral-feature classifiers (random forest, RBF-SVM, and gradient-boosted trees) reach at most 0.664 Macro F1 under the identical protocol, indicating that the task is not trivially separable. Because the 90 folds are not independent, significance is assessed with the subject as the unit ( $n{=}10$ ), which places the MS-MBSP mean in a  $95{\,}\%$  confidence interval of  $[0.701,{\,}0.821]$ . All data were collected from ten healthy adults seated in a single laboratory environment under instructed breathing, so these results should be read as a controlled structural comparison of CSI-based respiratory classifiers rather than as evidence of deployment-ready generalization.

title: MU-SHOT-Fi: Self-Supervised Multiuser Wi-Fi Sensing With Source-Free Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
abstract: Deep learning has been widely adopted for WiFi CSI-based human activity recognition (HAR) due to its ability to learn spatio-temporal features in a privacy-preserving and cost-effective manner. However, DL-based models generalize poorly across environments, a challenge that is amplified in multi-user settings where overlapping activities cause CSI entanglement and domain shifts. Moreover, practical deployments often limit access to labeled source data due to privacy constraints, motivating source-free adaptation using only unlabeled target-domain CSI and a pretrained source model. In this paper, we propose MU-SHOT-Fi, a source-free unsupervised domain adaptation framework for both single-user and multi-user Wi-Fi sensing scenarios. MU-SHOT-Fi employs permutation-invariant set prediction with Hungarian matching during source training, followed by frozen-classifier backbone adaptation in the target domain. To enable stable adaptation under domain shifts without labels, we introduce occupancy-weighted information maximization that prevents model collapse by focusing diversity regularization on likely-occupied slots while excluding the dominant class from marginal entropy. Additionally, we employ binary rotation prediction as spatial self-supervision that exploits CSI frequency-time structure to learn domain-invariant features. For single-user scenarios, we introduce SU-SHOT-Fi by customizing MU-SHOT-Fi through replacing occupancy weighting with standard information maximization and incorporating contrastive predictive coding to exploit temporal consistency. Extensive experiments are conducted on the multi-user WiMANS dataset and single-user Widar 3.0 dataset across cross-environment, cross-frequency, cross-orientation, and combined domain shifts. The results demonstrate that MU-SHOT-Fi effectively recovers multi-user exact-activity classification performance under large domain shifts while maintaining accurate occupancy estimation and preventing collapse toward dominant classes. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/AhmedRadwan02/mu-shot-fi.

title: MotionQ: Operator-Conditioned Motion Quotients for Cross-Observation WiFi Gesture Recognition
abstract: WiFi gesture recognition is accurate in fixed deployments but often degrades when user orientation, available links, or transceiver placement changes. Unlike ordinary domain shifts, these changes alter the wireless observation operator, so the same motion is expected to produce different measurements. Existing methods nevertheless pursue domain-invariant features and largely overlook changing layouts and observation configurations. Yet changing the observation operator also changes which task-relevant motion cues are physically observable, rather than merely altering the appearance of a fixed set of cues. Under a local linearization of the WiFi forward process, we derive a common task-observability condition under which a strict common linear representation is recoverable from every geometry-induced operator while preserving the gesture task. When the condition fails, enforcing stronger alignment across additional heterogeneous source operators may discard task-relevant cues still observable under individual operators. We therefore present MotionQ, which generates an operator-conditioned two-support motion measure for each candidate geometry. A motion quotient removes only the arbitrary ordering of its unlabeled supports and is represented by permutation-invariant central moments. Rather than matching quotients across operators, single-link-retention interventions encourage each view to retain information sufficient for gesture recognition. Extensive evaluations show that MotionQ is robust to extrapolative observation operators.

title: MuECNet: A Lightweight Multiuser Enhanced Convolutional Architecture for Robust CSI-Based Human Activity Recognition in Real-World IoT Environments
abstract: Wi-Fi Channel State Information (CSI)-based human activity recognition (HAR) leverages rich channel propagation characteristics to enable non-intrusive, privacy-preserving, and device-free sensing. In multi-user wireless environments, however, HAR faces significant challenges, including multi-path interference, signal overlap, label ambiguity, cross-domain channel variability, and constraints imposed by real-time deployment on resource-limited edge devices. This paper presents MuECNet (Multi-user Enhanced Convolutional Network), a lightweight and modular deep learning framework designed to operate under realistic multi-user, multi-activity CSI sensing conditions. MuECNet integrates three key components: (i) an Enhanced Convolutional Encoding Module (ECEM) for fine-grained temporal–spectral feature extraction that preserves channel propagation signatures; (ii) a Branch-wise Feature Normalization (BFN) module for user-specific channel representation learning; and (iii) an adaptive Decision Module for multi-label activity inference. To improve robustness under diverse and dynamic channel conditions, we introduce MixUp-based data augmentation to emulate activity overlap and reduce label ambiguity. Evaluations on the WiMANS dataset show that MuECNet achieves 64.46% (2.4 GHz) and 64.15% (5 GHz) accuracy with only 1.19M parameters, 1.74G FLOPs, and 0.28 s inference latency, outperforming baseline models such as ABLSTM and THAT while reducing model size by up to 75%. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each module, with accuracy drops of up to 6.41% when removed. These results demonstrate that MuECNet provides a robust and communication-efficient solution for integrating CSI-based sensing into future wireless networks and IoT systems.

title: Multimodal Information Fusion for Cross-domain WiFi-based Human Activity Recognition
venue: International Conference on Computer Supported Cooperative Work in Design (CSCWD)
abstract: The poor generalization caused by the environmental sensitivity of Channel State Information (CSI) remains a critical bottleneck in WiFi-based Human Activity Recognition (HAR). While existing data-centric and model-centric approaches attempt to mitigate this, they remain constrained by biases in limited seed samples or susceptibility to catastrophic forgetting in data-scarce scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose CrossTalk, a multimodal information fusion framework for cross-domain WiFi-based human activity recognition to enhance the generalization ability. The key is CrossTalk aligns CSI features with environment-independent text embeddings in a shared latent space. Moreover, by integrating CSI-text contrastive learning with a domain adaptation strategy, CrossTalk achieves an effective approach from passive fine-tuning to active semantic alignment. We validate CrossTalk on a public dataset spanning various spatial setups. Experimental results show that CrossTalk achieves superior generalization performance, particularly under few-shot scenarios.

title: Neural Approaches to Wi-Fi CSI-Based Human Activity Recognition: Architectures and Generalization
venue: IEEE Transactions on Cognitive Communications and Networking
abstract: WiFi-based passive sensing technology has become a key enabler in the rapidly advancing field of wireless communications, supporting a wide range of applications such as human activity recognition (HAR), gesture recognition, and indoor localization. Traditional WiFi sensing methods primarily rely on the received signal strength indicator (RSSI), which provides coarse-grained information and suffers from limited reliability. With the emergence of fine-grained channel state information (CSI), passive sensing using WiFi has achieved significant improvements in accuracy, robustness, and versatility. Recent advances in deep learning (DL) have greatly accelerated the development of WiFi CSI-based sensing, owing to its powerful capabilities in automatic feature extraction and complex pattern modeling. This survey provides a comprehensive and up-to-date overview of the latest developments in DL-based WiFi sensing techniques for HAR. The discussion begins with an overview of signal propagation characteristics and CSI acquisition methods, followed by a classification of sensing tasks based on data modalities and application scenarios. We then present a detailed review on commonly adopted neural network architectures, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), attention-based models, and Transformer variants. Furthermore, we examine recent methodological advancements such as domain adaptation, continual learning, and self-supervised learning. A comparative analysis highlights the strengths, limitations, and practical performance of various approaches. Finally, we discuss key challenges in the field, including cross-domain generalization, real-time processing, privacy concerns, and multi-modal fusion. We outline potential research directions to support the development of robust, scalable, and deployable WiFi sensing systems in real-world environments.

title: PDA-Fi: Device Placement Multi-SubDomain Adaptation for WiFi-based Human Sensing
abstract: Prior works show increasing potential in utilizing WiFi signals to capture the unique features of human body motions for human identification (HI) and human activity recognition (HAR). Existing works mostly employ the cross-domain deep learning models to lessen the discrepancy between the training and testing environment and mitigate the negative impact of several uncontrolled domains such as environment or walking trajectory. However, the WiFi device placement (deployed in various positions) incur significant domain shifts and bring multiple subdomains that not fully studied yet. In this paper, we propose a WiFi-based multi-subdomain adaptation human sensing system PDA-Fi that is able to eliminate the negative impact of WiFi device placement together with motion orientation and trajectory for activity and identity recognition applications. To lessen the difficulties of adapting multiple subdomains, PDA-Fi designs a novel dual-branch domain alignment model that divides overall source domains into two groups and aligns each group of subdomains with target domains to realize the coarse-grained domain adaptation. Next, PDA-Fi designs a cross-domain contrastive learning model to minimize distance between subdomains in each group and realize fine-grained domain adaptation. The comprehensive evaluation applied on 3 real-world public dataset shows PDA-Fi has well multi-subdomain adaptation performance in tackling device placement domain, as well as trajectories, orientations domains in both HI and HAR tasks and outperforms 7 state-of-the-art baselines.

title: PRoFENCH: A systematic study of multimodal fusion and generalization in WiFi–Vision wireless sensing for people counting
PULSE: Physics-Aware Temporal Embedding Learning for Domain Adaptive Wireless Sensing
abstract: We present PULSE, a lightweight domain-adaptive sensing framework that learns the physics-aware temporal embeddings, extracted from Wi-Fi channel frequency response (CFR). Unlike the existing approaches where the CFR is directly used as the input the tensor for Learning model, PULSE extracts temporal descriptors and embeds them through a light-weight 1D convolutional network that jointly learns discriminative representations and sensing semantics. The framework achieves over 99% accuracy while reducing 85% of the input tensor dimensionality and maintaining low inference latency, demonstrating suitability for real-time edge inference. Furthermore, through supervised contrastive pretraining and few-shot adaptation, PULSE generalizes effectively to unseen domains using only 5 s worth of labeled data, outperforming the state-of-the-art frameworks. We have extensively evaluated PULSE sensing framework with publicly available dataset of 20 different activities collected over multiple, subjects and propagation environment. For reproducibility, the code base will be made available at: https://github.com/rifatzabin/PULSE.

title: Parameterized synthetic WiFi CSI data generation for trustworthy human activity recognition: A Sim2Real approach with edge deployment analysis
Personalized Federated Learning for Cross-Domain Human Activity Recognition using Wi-Fi Sensing
abstract: Wi-Fi sensing based on Channel State Information (CSI) is a robust method for Human Activity Recognition (HAR). However, this method suffers from significant performance degradation in cross-domain scenarios because the system fails to generalize patterns across environments. This research proposes applying a Personalized Federated Learning framework to address this problem, using the Generalized Total Variation Minimization (GTVMin) principle. The proposed approach aims to obtain an optimal model for each domain by collaboratively training custom CNN-BiLSTM models using graphs that capture the statistical similarities of the CSI channel across domains, prioritizing specialization over generalization. The proposed framework promotes consensus across related domains through a regularization term that balances each local model with the related domains. The results demonstrate that applying GTVMin in HAR, using statistical similarity graphs of the CSI channel, not only outperforms isolated local models, but also significantly improves performance over centralized and averaged approaches.

title: PhiFi: Physics-informed deep learning for wi-fi-based human activity recognition
abstract: The rapid proliferation of Wireless Fidelity (Wi-Fi) sensing technology faces significant challenges related to trustworthiness and robustness, particularly when deployed in unpredictable environments with noisy labels. Although deep learning approaches have achieved high accuracy, they often lack physical interpretability and may fail catastrophically under distributional shifts. To address these limitations, we introduce PhiFi, a physics-informed deep learning framework that integrates electromagnetic principles-specifically, the Helmholtz wave equation-through a supervised Physics Head and Residual Gating mechanism for device-free human activity recognition. Our framework improves calibration consistency, achieving an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of 2.84% on synthetic data (SRV protocol, compared to 3.39% for purely data-driven baselines). On real-world UT-HAR benchmark data, calibration reaches 4.1% (LOSO cross-domain protocol), matching the baseline's cross-domain generalization (≈84% macro-F1) while demonstrating improved label efficiency in extreme scarcity regimes (1% labels: +25.7 pp improvement under STEA protocol). Comprehensive evaluations across synthetic stress conditions and real benchmark datasets indicate that physics-informed constraints provide a practical approach for improving model trustworthiness and calibration, offering potential benefits for safety-critical Internet of Things (IoT) applications in data-limited scenarios.

title: Physics-Informed Wi-Fi Channel State Information Sensing for Device-Free Human Activity Recognition: A Survey
abstract: Wi-Fichannel state information (CSI) enables non-intrusive device-free human activity recognition (DFHAR) on commodity wireless infrastructure, yet the electromagnetic sensitivity that resolves sub-millimeter motion makes trained models fragile to environment, hardware, and user change. Prior surveys treat cross-domain adaptation, physics-informed modeling, self-supervised learning, and edge deployment largely in isolation and seldom explain how measurement inconsistency, information loss, and distributional shift interact as coupled failure modes. This survey synthesizes the Wi-Fi CSI DFHAR corpus through three lenses—physics-constrained learning, information-theoretic compression, and cross-domain adaptation—and interprets reported results under matched protocol attributes. Physics-informed residuals in the reviewed literature primarily act as training-time regularizers: they help mainly under scarce labels and a residual commensurate with the CSI grid, and become redundant or harmful when labels already fit the task or the operator is not identifiable from commodity measurements. A structured extraction schema and a dry-run/pilot/sustain commissioning playbook are offered as reporting templates for auditable wireless sensing deployments.

title: Privacy-Preserving Wi-Fi Multi-User Sensing Through Data Poisoning
abstract: Wi-Fi human sensing, boosted by latest progress in both system innovation and deep analytics, has demonstrated ever-increasing resolution of users’ activities. Nonetheless, it may become a spy on users’ private activities such as password entry or intimate social interactions. Existing countermeasures include signal obfuscation and adversarial perturbations to hamper and confuse Wi-Fi sensing, yet they both require substantial changes in Wi-Fi hardware/firmware, and they at most stay at user level in protection granularity. This paper presents Poison2Cure, the first semantic-level privacy-preserving framework for Wi-Fi human sensing systems, with full compatibility to any underlying hardware. The innovation behind Poison2Cure lies in feeding poisoned training data from (privacy-sensitive) users to the neural model for Wi-Fi sensing, degrading only the sensing for private activities while retaining that for regular ones. Moreover, we extend this framework to scenarios where the neural model is confidential, addressing incomplete cooperation in Wi-Fi sensing systems. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that Poison2Cure reduces over 76% of the accuracy for the private activities while keeping the accuracy for regular activities largely intact.

title: ProFi-Net: Prototype-Based Feature Attention with Curriculum Augmentation for WiFi-Based Gesture Recognition
RePos: Relative-to-Absolute Pose Factorization for Cross-Environment WiFi-Based 3D Human Pose Estimation
abstract: Device-free 3D human pose estimation from commodity WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) enables human sensing that preserves privacy and tolerates poor illumination, but its deployment is limited by poor generalization across environments. Unlike images, CSI measurements have no spatially localized correspondence to body parts and are heavily affected by multipath propagation. Consequently, models that regress absolute poses entangle body structure with location cues specific to each environment. Within a single environment this coupling is not problematic: RePos-D, a direct model that regresses the absolute pose, already achieves the best reported accuracy on Person-in-WiFi-3D, a 3.4% gain over the previous best WiFi method, DT-Pose. Across environments, however, the same model overfits position and degrades sharply. We therefore propose RePos, a factorized framework that separates root-relative pose estimation from root localization. By shielding the structure branch from absolute position, RePos learns robust pose representations. Specifically, it groups CSI features into latent tokens organized by body part that a skeleton-guided module refines into the pose, while a separate network estimates the root position from CSI amplitude through a differentiable spatial decomposition. Under the strict MM-Fi cross-environment protocol, RePos reduces the mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) by 10-21% over existing WiFi methods. The improvement is consistent across activity protocols, holds when each environment is held out in turn, and survives few-shot transfer without data leakage. Further analysis shows that the relative pose predictions remain largely independent of position, whereas root localization remains dependent on the environment.

title: Research on Cross-Domain Gesture Recognition Method Based on WiFi CSI and Deep Learning
venue: International Conference on Computer Information Science and Application Technology (CISAT)
abstract: WiFi CSI-based cross-domain gesture recognition faces significant challenges, including feature distribution shifts, poor model generalization, and overfitting. To mitigate these issues, this paper proposes an efficient cross-domain gesture recognition method specifically designed for single-transceiver links. First, we introduce a progressive time-domain preprocessing scheme that employs empirical mode decomposition and kurtosis-based adaptive filtering to effectively mitigate environmental pulses and hardware noise. A variance-based subcarrier selection mechanism is employed to identify the most discriminative core subcarriers. Second, one-dimensional CSI amplitude sequences are mapped into 2D recurrence plots, thereby preserving inter-subcarrier correlations and enhancing the robustness of cross-domain features. Third, we propose a cross-domain adversarial network EfficientNetB0-SCFM-DANN(SDEB). This architecture employs a lightweight EfficientNetB0 as the backbone, integrates a spatial-channel feature modulator (SCFM) into the deep layers to refine discriminative gesture features and mitigate background interference, and cascades a domain adversarial neural network (DANN) with gradient reversal to extract domain-invariant representations. In cross-environment experiments—specifically, training in a meeting room and corridor while testing in an office—the proposed method achieves an accuracy of 90.13% across five distinct gestures (circle, hand raising, X, wave, and W), underscoring its significant robustness and generalization capabilities in complex cross-domain scenarios.

title: Research on Human Action Recognition Based on WiFi CSI Using Improved Parallel Neural Network
abstract: Device-free human activity recognition (HAR) using WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) offers a low-cost and privacy-preserving sensing solution. However, existing deep learning approaches often rely on generic architectures that underutilize multi-domain physical features and incur prohibitive computational overhead for edge devices. In this letter, we propose a lightweight, task-oriented parallel neural network tailored for WiFi sensing. Specifically, high-resolution Doppler Frequency Shift (DFS) features are explicitly extracted to capture fine-grained human kinematics. These are jointly modeled alongside temporal and spatial dynamics using a three-branch architecture comprising attention-enhanced bidirectional GRUs and a channel-attention CNN module. Furthermore, an adaptive attention-gated mechanism is introduced for optimal multi-domain feature fusion. Extensive experiments on the public UT-HAR dataset yield a state-of-the-art accuracy of 98.49%. Additional evaluations on the highly challenging, cross-domain Widar dataset demonstrate an accuracy of 83.33%, substantially outperforming classical and heavy-weight vision baselines (e.g., ResNet18 and ViT). Requiring only 4.92 M parameters and 98.72 M FLOPs, the proposed framework achieves a superior trade-off between recognition precision and computational efficiency, validating its immense potential for practical, resource-constrained WiFi sensing applications.

title: SALxO: Semantic Augmentation via Latent-Space Exploration
venue: IEEE Wireless Communications and Networking Conference Workshops (WCNCW)
abstract: Recent advances in wireless networks have spurred interest in using Wi-Fi signals for human-centric mobile sensing tasks, such as gesture recognition and activity detection. To address the scarcity of labeled data in these applications, researchers increasingly turn to self-supervised learning (SSL) techniques for representation learning. In parallel, deep generative models, e.g., generative adversarial networks (GANs) and diffusion models, have been used to expand wireless sensing datasets via synthetic data generation. However, these efforts often treat generative models as black-box data expanders, with limited attention to semantic context or augmentation quality. In this paper, we propose a novel augmentation method termed the semantic augmentation via latent-space exploration (SALxO), which leverages the latent space of a variational auto-encoder (VAE) to generate semantically consistent views for contrastive learning. SALxO uses a latent chaining algorithm that traverses structured regions of the latent manifold, producing meaningful positive pairs without labels or handcrafted perturbations. Integrated into fixed SimCLR and AutoFi backbones, SALxO improves few-shot accuracy by up to 13 % and accelerates convergence, without requiring architecture changes. These results highlight SALxO's promise for scalable and label-efficient SSL-enabled wireless sensing.

title: SD 2 A-Net: Attention-Enhanced Static–Dynamic Wi-Fi CSI Decomposition for Cross-Domain Human Activity Recognition
abstract: Wi-Fi-based device-free Human Activity Recognition (HAR) faces significant performance degradation in unseen environments due to dominant environment-dependent (static) components in Channel State Information (CSI). We propose SD²A-Net (Static–Dynamic Decomposition with Attention Network), a robust cross-domain framework that decouples motion-induced dynamics from background interference. The framework utilizes a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) on CSI amplitude to isolate motion-related variations and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on CSI phase to suppress low-rank environmental structures. These refined features are processed via a Dual-stream Attention-CNN to capture global temporal dependencies and local hierarchical patterns. Evaluations on MultiEnv, Widar 3.0, and a self-collected MINE Lab dataset demonstrate superior generalization. SD²A-Net achieves average cross-environment accuracies of 84.91% and 81.90% on MultiEnv and Widar 3.0, respectively, while achieving average cross-subject accuracies of 90.60% and 88.10% on MultiEnv and the MINE Lab dataset, respectively. These results confirm that explicit static–dynamic decomposition combined with multi-scale attention significantly enhances the robustness and scalability of Wi-Fi HAR systems under large domain shifts.

title: SHARP: Environment and Person Independent Activity Recognition
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This research proposal introduces SHARP, a framework dedicated to achieving Environment and Person Independent Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using Wi-Fi Channel State Information (CSI). The primary challenge in wireless sensing is the performance drop when models encounter new users or unfamiliar physical settings (Domain Shift). SHARP addresses this by focusing on the extraction of robust, physical-layer Doppler features that remain invariant across different subjects and environments. By implementing a specialized signal processing pipeline to mitigate multipath interference and hardware noise, this work aims to provide a scalable and reliable solution for real-world ambient intelligence applications. This work is published as a research preprint to facilitate further development in the field of cross-domain wireless sensing.

title: Scene-Adaptive Continual Learning for CSI-based Human Activity Recognition with Mixture of Experts
abstract: Channel state information (CSI)-based human activity recognition (HAR) is vulnerable to performance degradation under domain shifts across varying physical environments. Continual learning (CL) offers a principled way to learn new domains sequentially while preserving past knowledge, but existing CL solutions for CSI-based HAR scale poorly with accumulating domains, rely on a large replay buffer, or incur linearly growing inference cost. In this letter, we propose Scene-Adaptive Mixture of Experts with Clustered Specialists (SAMoE-C), which formulates cross-domain CSI-based HAR as a mixture-of-experts system that enables scene-specific adaptation, via an attention-based semantic router that activates only selected experts for each input. Moreover, we develop a novel training protocol, which requires only a tiny replay buffer for stabilizing domain discrimination of the router. Experimental results on a four-scene CSI dataset demonstrate that SAMoE-C approaches the state-of-the-art accuracy, while maintaining a significantly lower inference cost. By jointly combining modular experts, selective activation with router and a lightweight training protocol, SAMoE-C enables scalable cross-domain CSI-based HAR deployment with low training overhead and high computational efficiency in real-world settings.

title: Self-Supervised Wi-Fi Activity Recognition via Iterative Pseudo-Labeling
abstract: With the rapid advancement of the Internet of Things (IoT) and smart environments, Wi-Fi-based human activity recognition has made significant progress, providing nonintrusive and flexible sensing capabilities. However, most existing methods still depend on manual annotations, which severely limits their scalability and practicality in real-world scenarios where labeled data is scarce or unavailable. To address this, we propose LISAR, a novel two-stage iterative self-supervised Wi-Fi activity recognition framework that learns from unlabeled data. Specifically, we introduce a contrastive pretraining approach by training with the proposed composite loss function, co-InfoNCE loss, and a physics-informed data augmentation strategy to learn discriminative representations from unlabeled data. In addition, we design a pseudo-label confidence-guided iterative self-supervised learning (PC-ISL) module. Through iterative updates, this module refines pseudo-labels and enables efficient data utilization, thereby enhancing the model’s discrimination on unlabeled data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LISAR achieves high-accuracy activity recognition while relying strictly on unlabeled data for representation learning, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art self-supervised methods.

title: Solving the WiFi Sensing Dilemma in Reality Leveraging Conformal Prediction
abstract: With the extensive deployment of smart environments and IoT devices, WiFi sensing has proven its significant convenience and contact-free sensing capabilities in supporting a wide range of applications. However, designing a ubiquitous WiFi sensing system for diverse real-world scenarios presents a substantial dilemma, as the system performance deteriorates when the testing data diverges significantly from the training data due to domain variations. To address this dilemma, existing studies need extra efforts to develop new features or even retrain the original model under environmental variations. However, these approaches have not efficiently resolved the dilemma. In this study, we conduct a comprehensive study on the domain variation problem to make WiFi sensing robust and accurate in practical applications.
